doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Teaching scales and analysis rather than names
summary: On the Guitar Grimoire, scale catalogues and why he makes students analyze what they play.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. What if I came to you as a student and said “Carmen, when should I use a symmetric diminished scale?”
I would say “what have you been reading?”
I ask that because it’s been asked of me and I didn’t know how to respond.

I have a book called The Grimoire, The Guitar Grimoire. And I didn’t know this before, but grimoire is an ancient word which means a manual, a magician’s manual. I mean you open it up and you have all these spells. That kind of stuff. And it is hundreds of diagrams, all over the neck of the guitar, and notation, on all these various scales and their names. You know, the Arabian scale, the Hungarian sharp two scale, I mean these things go on and on and on and on. And there are a lot of people that take great pride in saying okay here’s a scale and we’ll make this change and that change and now we’ll give it this name and we’ll do the modes of those scales, which on guitar translates to seven different finger patterns, so even a major scale would consist of seven different notes, now is 49 different locations in the first octave alone, so you learn all these patterns. Then you try to tell the guy, “where’s the C?” “Oh wait a minute. Hang on. I’ll tell you in a minute.” And he’ll locate it. So again, the guitar is a graphic animal and you have to approach it in a different way. But what these guys have done is come up with all of these variations on the scale until you can use this scale over this chord, and this over that and this over that. So in a way there’s a certain understandable value to that. But on the other hand you can’t just learn a catalogue of scales and say “okay, this is going to be Enigmatic scale.” “Right, well how do I use it?” “Well let’s see how somebody else used it.” And you find that, at least for me, it comes out to be building melodies. And you build melodies based on active notes, notes that are not in the chord but have a little bit, of a tension that takes you someplace; and on passive notes, which are nice resolve notes, and it depends on what you want to create. So if you want to create a whole bunch of active notes then you can play a scale a half-step below where it’s supposed to be and say “isn’t that cool?” Then you have to look at it and say does that mean anything? Am I playing something just because it’s tense, or am I playing something because I want to © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -17-

have a little tension which takes me to a nice resolve. So you have to start thinking about how you want to do things. So I’d say a lot of academics in music I have found is learning a lot of names, spitting them back on the test, and then, without a full understanding of what those elements are supposed to do musically they’re meaningless. You get people that just use these scales and they don’t really know why and they can’t make any music out of them. So I tell them “if you want to learn the names, that’s cool. But I want you to listen to what are you playing, why are you playing it, how does that fit and where are you going with it. Is it something you played before. Are you playing that motif backwards, what are you doing?” I get them to analyze what they’re playing and how they do it.

I’m beginning to see why all the guitar players in town say “you have to go to Carmen.” That’s great, what you just said. Do you ever tell a student that — do you ever use the word “mistake” when you’re listening to a student try to improvise?

If it’s actually a mistake. I try to make a distinction between did you mean to play this note or did you just hit it wrong. If you hit it wrong, that’s a mistake. If you meant to play it then let’s talk about why you did that.
